title: Measuring whether a review template helped, in SQL
summary: Twelve documented PostgreSQL queries over a synthetic review queue, built to answer one question: did a template make reviews faster without making them worse?

stat.label: over 1,800 synthetic reviews, with a data-quality check that must return zero rows

sections.heading: Problem
paragraphs: A team rolls out a checklist template and wants to know if it worked. Saying reviews feel faster is not enough, and one average can hide a mix shift, a slow tail or a drop in quality. I wanted a worked example of the questions I ask before I report a result like that.

sections.heading: What I built
paragraphs: A synthetic review queue in PostgreSQL: 6 reviewers, 1,800 applications and 1,800 reviews from a fixed random seed. The template reaches one reviewer per week, so every reviewer has work before and after it. The repository holds the schema, the seed, twelve commented queries and a script that rebuilds everything and exits non-zero if the row count is wrong.

The queries cover volume by month, median and 90th-percentile time, the comparison by category, a weekly trend with a rolling mean, adoption by reviewer, rework, outcome mix, channel, hours saved, a window-function ranking, and a check for reviews that start before their application arrives.

sections.heading: Result
paragraphs: In the synthetic data, median review time fell from 28.1 to 10.8 minutes. Every category fell by at least 60%, so the drop is not a mix shift. Rework fell from 9.6% to 6.5%. The staggered start shows up as a step down across six weeks.
The data is synthetic and I built the speedup into the generator, so this is a demonstration of method, not evidence that a real template works. The write-up says so at the top.

sections.heading: What the data showed that I had to explain
paragraphs: Denials rose from 17.7% to 21.5% after the template. The generator draws outcomes at the same rate in both groups, so the gap is sampling noise, and I wrote that down. On real data, an outcome shift next to a speedup is the first thing to investigate, because a faster review that decides differently is a change in the decision, not only in the speed.

sections.heading: Lesson
paragraphs: Report the median and the tail, split by category, and check outcomes and rework beside speed. Add a query that must return zero rows, so a broken join cannot pass as a clean result.

sources: samples/sql-reporting in this repository: schema.sql, seed.sql, queries.sql and results.txt from a run on PostgreSQL 16
